practice1.prompt: Starting from names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Cleo"], write each name on its own line into names.txt, then print Wrote 3 names

cases.name: the names are written to the file, not printed
cases.describe: open() and write() putting the names in the file

cases.name: the list is walked rather than typed out three times
cases.describe: a for loop over the names

hiddenCases.name: names.txt has all three names, one per line
hiddenCases.describe: names.txt with Alice, Bob and Cleo on separate lines

practice1.hint: Two things trip this up: write() does not add a newline of its own, and a file opened in write mode starts empty every single time it is opened.

questions.prompt: What does file.write("Alice") followed by file.write("Bob") put in the file?
questions.explain: write() writes exactly the characters you gave it. If you want a line break you have to write one.

questions.prompt: You open a file in "w" mode inside a loop, once per name. What ends up in the file?
questions.explain: Each open in write mode empties the file again, so every pass throws away the pass before it. Open once, outside the loop.

questions.prompt: Match each job to the mode that suits it.
left: Adding a line to a log
Saving a report that replaces yesterday's
questions.explain: A log grows, so it appends. A report supersedes the old one, so it writes. Settings are only being looked at, so they are read.

questions.prompt: What does writelines(['a', 'b']) put in the file?
questions.explain: Despite the name, writelines adds no newlines. The strings you pass have to carry their own.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Say what happens to yesterday's contents under each mode, then give a real file that would want each one.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Walk the list, write each student, and say explicitly what puts the next one on a new line.
